[/page/3/Text/5] In order to explore the pathways to and from suicide attempts in the past and after release from prison, we carried out a qualitative interview study. We used the prison system as a point for obtaining our sample and interviewed 35 male offenders, aged 18–52, 1 week prior to and approximately 6 weeks after their release from a Category B medium secure prison in South-West England (Howerton et al. 2007).[/page/3/Text/6] We over-sampled young offenders and those categorised by the prison assessment care in custody teamwork system as being at risk of suicide.[/page/3/Text/7] The pre-release interview included questions about the participants' childhood and early history, methods of coping with stress and difficulties, previous suicide attempts, perception of their own mental health, and attitudes towards help seeking. The post-release interview included a discussion of recent life events, current mental distress and any suicidal thoughts or attempts following release.

Of those who admitted having attempted suicide at some time, about half had made only one attempt (around a quarter of the sample). In this group, we also included two individuals who had had close encounters with suicide without having made an actual attempt on their life. One man had climbed onto the rail of a high bridge and was eventually coaxed down by a passer-by. Another, Simon, had carried a gun around for a year, contemplating suicide.

Of those who admitted having attempted suicide at some time, about half had made only one attempt (around a quarter of the sample). [/page/3/Text/3] This article, part of a wider study of prison leavers' mental health needs (Howerton et al. 2007), addresses two specific research questions with a view to informing suicide prevention strategies, namely: how do offenders explain their own and others' suicide attempts? And what leads some offenders, but not others, to attempt suicide?

Suicide is common among offenders, who are at increased risk of homelessness, unemployment and mental illness and are prone to impulsivity. Release from prison is a particularly vulnerable time. ... Multiple attempters were often in despair and enmeshed in substance misuse, with little control over their lives. ... Most of those with one-off or no previous attempts portrayed themselves as having more mastery. ... Projective agency, having a more future orientation, appeared more prominent in some single attempters and in those individuals with plans to escape crime and social exclusion.

Most of the respondents described tumultuous personal histories, 24 having experienced family break-down or abandonment as children, 26 recounting tales of physical abuse or neglect and 15 of excessive drug and alcohol use in their family homes. All reported recent personal problems. ... Our first observation was that, as they talked about their past lives and described their hopes and plans for the future, those who had made only one attempt generally presented themselves as having more control of their lives than those who had made multiple attempts. In terms of their perceived control, or mastery, as exhibited in their spoken responses, they appeared similar to most of those who had never attempted suicide.

Risk: 'It was also clear that they had been prompted by a specific adverse event, or unusually low or distressing period.' Recovery: 'They portrayed themselves as exercising a degree of judgement on the suicide attempts and in their lives, as well as describing an ability to reflect on and learn from past problems.' and 'They generally described clear plans for the future and a sense of purpose'.

Their future lives are in the balance, their uncertain talk does not rule out the possibility that some future event will push them to take their lives, or that recreational drug use will shift to habit and then necessity, or that past traumas or sense of abandonment will resurface and swallow their vitality. (Risk) --- For Simon, who had carried a gun around for a year, contemplating suicide, the crisis and its resolution were still of great significance but his family ties made him realise he had a will to live. (Recovery) --- I have been able to recognise points where I know that I'm going to have to pick up the phone and talk to somebody, other than just the Samaritans, someone that I would want to help.... I feel I have more control over myself now than I did before, yeah. Because I've woken up to responsibility, I've woken up to the fact that I know the answer's not in the bottom of a glass, I've woken up to the fact that not everybody out there hates me, not every phone call I make for a job is going to be a no, not every person I speak to is going to think of me as a bit of muck. (Recovery)

Risk: despairing narratives, expressed by most offenders with multiple suicide attempts as well as by the 'no balls' offenders are inextricably linked to damaged identities and restricted agency (Nelson 2001). Recovery: The one-offs appeared determined not to make further attempts, and yet had often used violent means such as hanging, which require significant future-orientated planning and can be seen as involving projective agency or autonomous reflexivity, the latter linked to relatively quick and independent decision-making. For some, cycles of despair and further, more habitual suicide attempts continue; for others, life events, including the suicide attempt itself, might bring about 'narrative repair' (Palmer 2007: 371), and this new narrative might be interpreted as mastery.
